quests.d: Count how many keys hash % N really moves, size up the hash space, look a key up in code, and find exactly which keys move when a server joins or leaves
quests.goal: Your win today: you can put numbers on the rehashing problem (adding 1 server to N moves about N/(N+1) of keys with % N, but only about 1/(N+1) on a ring), explain the hash space and how arcs become ownership shares, sketch the lookup as a binary search over sorted positions, and walk an interviewer through exactly which keys move, and from which server, when a node joins or leaves.
quests.bookSections: Ch. 5: The rehashing problem; Consistent hashing (definition, k/n); Hash space and hash ring; Hash servers; Hash keys; Server lookup; Add a server; Remove a server; Find affected keys (both cases).

stages.title: Do the rehash math
stages.sub: Put an exact number on 'most keys move'
stages.teaches: Book setup: N cache servers, pick one with serverIndex = hash(key) % N. Works while N never changes. When a server is added or removed, N changes, so most keys get a new index; in a cache those keys are now looked up on the wrong server, so a wave of cache misses falls through to the database. Exact math (new to this quest, 0002 only shows it visually): for uniformly random hashes, a key keeps its server when going N -> N+1 only if hash % N equals hash % (N+1), which happens for 1 key in N+1. So modulo moves N/(N+1) of keys: 4->5 moves 80%, 9->10 moves 90%, 99->100 moves 99%. Shrinking N -> N-1 moves (N-1)/N: 4->3 moves 75%. Consistent hashing, by contrast, only moves about k/n keys on average (k = number of keys, n = number of slots/servers): adding the (N+1)th server moves about 1/(N+1) of keys, removing one of N moves about 1/N (just the dead server's share). Key insight: modulo gets WORSE as the cluster grows, the ring gets BETTER. Second subtle point: after a removal, the servers are renumbered (0..N-2), so 'server 1 died' also shifts every index above it; that is part of why the mapping scrambles.
stages.interaction: Part A, hand calculation (calculate-and-check). A table of 8 user keys with small made-up hash values (do NOT copy the book's table): alice 1044, bob 2208, carol 3917, dave 4521, erin 5374, frank 6610, grace 7085, heidi 8862. Column 1 (hash % 4) is pre-filled: 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2. The banner says 'One of the 4 cache servers died, so N = 3.' For each row the learner taps 0 / 1 / 2 to fill hash % 3 (correct: 0, 0, 2, 0, 1, 1, 2, 0). A wrong tap shakes and shows the division (e.g. '3917 = 3 x 1305 + 2'). When all 8 are filled, rows whose server changed turn red and a counter shows '6 of 8 keys moved (75%)'. Then the learner types a prediction for 'With a ring instead, how many of these 8 keys would move on average?' (accept 2; explain: only the dead server's ~1/4 share). Part B, the curve. A slider N = 2..100 and a small two-line chart (x = cluster size N, y = % of keys moved when one server is added): red line N/(N+1) for % N, green line 1/(N+1) for the ring, with readouts at the slider value. Predict-then-watch: before unlocking the slider, ask 'At N = 50, adding one server moves what share of keys with % N?' options 'About 2%' / 'About 50%' / 'About 98%' (correct: about 98%). Then the slider reveals the curves. Add a small 'See it with 100 keys' link to Quest 6.2 stage 1 (lessons/0002-consistent-hashing.html) for the colour-grid version.
stages.check: All 8 hash % 3 cells correct; prediction made; Q.quiz: 'A 20-server cache using hash % N adds one server. Roughly what share of cached keys now miss?' options 'About 5%' / 'About 50%' / 'About 95%' -> correct 'About 95%' (20/21). Good-feedback mentions a ring would move about 1/21, under 5%.

stages.title: Bend the number line
stages.sub: Hash space, hash ring, and what an arc is worth
stages.teaches: Hash space: every value a hash function can output. The book's example uses SHA-1, whose output runs from 0 to 2^160 - 1 (2^160 is about 1.46 x 10^48). Join the two ends of that number line and you get the hash ring. Servers are hashed (by IP address or name) onto the ring; keys are hashed onto the same ring with the same function, with no modulo step. A server's partition is the arc between the previous server (anticlockwise) and itself; the share of keys it gets is that arc length divided by the whole space. Arc formula with wrap-around: share = ((pos_server - pos_prev) mod S) / S, where S is the size of the space. Why such a huge space? So that positions practically never collide: with a trillion (10^12) keys the chance that any two share a SHA-1 position is about n^2 / 2^161, roughly 3 x 10^-25. Real systems: Amazon Dynamo hashes keys with MD5 (128-bit space); Cassandra's default Murmur3Partitioner uses 64-bit signed tokens from -2^63 to 2^63 - 1. Ring size doesn't change the idea, only the resolution.
stages.interaction: Opening animation: a horizontal number line labelled 0 ... 2^160 - 1 curls into a circle (the two ends meet at the top, labelled '2^160 - 1 | 0'). Then a toy 8-bit space 0..255 replaces it (labels in decimal, with angle = pos / 256 x 360). Three calculate-and-check cards, each drawn on the toy ring: (1) Two servers, s0 at 64 and s1 at 192. 'What share of keys does s1 own?' number input in % -> 50 (arc 64..192 = 128/256). (2) Three servers s0 at 32, s1 at 112, s2 at 240. 'Share of s0?' -> 18.75% (arc from 240 wraps through 0 to 32 = 48/256); a wrong answer animates the wrap-around arc in colour and shows the mod formula. (3) 'A key hashes to 250. Which server stores it?' tap s0/s1/s2 -> s0 (walk clockwise, wrap past 0). After the cards, a 'Scale it up' panel shows the same arcs relabelled in SHA-1 units (e.g. 2^158 for a quarter of the ring) and the collision maths as a one-line reveal.
stages.check: All three cards correct (wrong answers cost a heart but allow retry); Q.quiz: 'Why does the book use a hash space as large as 0 to 2^160 - 1?' options 'So positions basically never collide, and keys spread smoothly around the ring' / 'So the ring can hold at most 2^160 servers' / 'Because bigger hash values are faster to compare' -> first.

stages.title: Clockwise, in code
stages.sub: Server lookup is a binary search with a wrap
stages.teaches: The book describes lookup as 'walk clockwise from the key until you hit a server'. Nobody literally walks: an implementation keeps the server positions (tokens) in a sorted array and binary-searches for the first position >= the key's hash. If the hash is larger than every token, the walk wraps past the top of the ring, so the answer is the first (smallest) token. Lookup is O(log T) for T tokens: 256,000 tokens (1,000 servers x 256 virtual nodes) needs about 18 comparisons. Boundary convention matters: a key that lands exactly on a server position belongs to that server (>=). The ring itself is tiny metadata that every client or router keeps a copy of; it changes only when membership changes.
stages.interaction: Part A, trace it. Sorted tokens [12, 40, 71, 93] in a 0..99 toy ring (s0..s3), drawn as both an array and a ring. Four keys appear one at a time: 5, 40, 41, 97. For each, the learner taps the owning token in the array. Correct answers: 5 -> 12, 40 -> 40 (exactly on it, >= rule), 41 -> 71, 97 -> wrap -> 12. After each tap, the binary search animates (lo/mid/hi pointers moving over the array) and the ring shows the clockwise walk. Part B, spot the bug. Show this 8-line function and ask 'Which line gives the wrong server for key 97?': line 1 'function lookup(tokens, h) {  // tokens sorted ascending', line 2 '  let lo = 0, hi = tokens.length - 1;', line 3 '  while (lo < hi) {', line 4 '    const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;', line 5 '    if (tokens[mid] < h) lo = mid + 1;', line 6 '    else hi = mid;', line 7 '  }', line 8 '  return tokens[lo];'. Correct: line 2 (or line 8 also accepted): with hi = length - 1, a hash above the last token returns 93, which is anticlockwise of the key. Reveal the fix: hi = tokens.length and return tokens[lo % tokens.length]. One heart per wrong line tap; explanation shown either way.
stages.check: All four traces correct and the bug found; Q.quiz: 'Your ring has 1,000 servers with 256 virtual nodes each. About how many comparisons does one lookup take?' options 'About 18' / 'About 1,000' / 'About 256,000' -> about 18 (log2 256,000).

stages.title: Who has to move?
stages.sub: The book's method for finding affected keys
stages.teaches: Book's step-by-step rule. Adding a server: start at the new server and go anticlockwise until you reach the previous server; every key in that arc moves to the new server, and they all come from the new server's clockwise neighbour (the server that used to own the arc). Removing a server: start at the removed server and go anticlockwise until the previous server; every key in that arc moves to the removed server's clockwise neighbour. Nothing else on the ring changes. Ops consequence: when a node joins a real store, you know exactly which source to stream data from, and the transfer is bounded to one arc. With virtual nodes (link to Quest 6.2 stage 4 for the lab) the same rule runs once per virtual node, so a joining server pulls a small arc from several different servers, and a leaving server hands small arcs to several servers. That spreads the copy work, which is good for speed and for not overloading one neighbour.
stages.interaction: 'Highlighter' sim on a 0..99 toy ring. Servers A at 10, B at 35, C at 60, D at 85. Twelve keys at 3, 14, 22, 30, 41, 47, 55, 63, 70, 78, 88, 95, coloured by owner (first server at position >= key, wrapping). Three rounds. In each, the change is shown as a dashed ghost; the learner taps every key they think will move (taps toggle a yellow ring), then taps the server they will move FROM / TO when asked, then presses 'Apply'. The sim then animates the anticlockwise sweep from the changed server back to the previous server, highlighting the arc, and scores: +XP per correct key, -1 heart per false positive or missed key (max one heart per round). Round 1 (add E at 50): moving keys 41, 47; from C to E. Round 2 (remove A at 10): moving keys 88, 95, 3 (the arc wraps past 0); all to B. Round 3 (add E with 3 virtual nodes at 20, 50, 90 on the original ring): moving keys 14 (from B), 41 and 47 (from C), 88 (from A); the learner must tag each moved key with its source. After round 3, a counter shows: 4 of 12 keys moved, pulled from 3 different servers, versus round 1 where one server gave up everything.
stages.check: All three rounds completed; Q.quiz: 'Server X is removed from a basic ring (one position per server). Which keys move?' options 'The keys between X and the server anticlockwise of it; they go to X's clockwise neighbour' / 'The keys between X and the server clockwise of it; they go to X's anticlockwise neighbour' / 'Every key on the ring is re-hashed' -> first.

stages.title: Boss: The Migration Planner
stages.sub: Who has to stream data for this change?
stages.teaches: Applying 'find affected keys' to real operations, including two traps: changing the hash function re-maps nearly everything (every key and server gets a new position), and hashing servers by something unstable (like an IP address that changes on reboot) makes a server jump to a new spot, which is a remove plus an add.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with 3 choices: { k: 'one', label: 'One neighbour', sub: 'a single server hands over or takes over one arc' }, { k: 'few', label: 'A few servers, a little each', sub: 'several small arcs change hands' }, { k: 'all', label: 'Nearly every key moves', sub: 'the mapping is scrambled' }. Seven scenarios: (1) Basic ring, one position per server; a new server joins -> one (only its clockwise neighbour gives up an arc). (2) Ring with 128 virtual nodes per server; a new server joins -> few (it takes a small arc next to each of its 128 positions, from many different servers). (3) Cache clients use hash(key) % 12; ops adds a 13th box -> all (12/13, about 92%, remap). (4) Basic ring; a server is removed for maintenance -> one (its clockwise neighbour receives its whole arc). (5) Virtual-node ring; a server crashes -> few (its slices scatter to many servers). (6) You switch the ring's hash function from SHA-1 to Murmur3 to save CPU -> all (every key and every server lands somewhere new; plan this like a full migration). (7) Servers are placed on the ring by hashing their IP; a basic-ring server reboots and gets a new IP -> few (its old arc goes to one neighbour and its new arc is taken from another: a remove plus an add; that's why you hash a stable server ID). Outro: 'Count the arcs that change. One position = one neighbour; many virtual nodes = a little from many; a new N or a new hash function = everything.'
stages.check: Q.boss round completed under the engine's hearts rules.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.sub: Explain a node join, with numbers
stages.teaches: Model answer pulls together the quest: the math, the lookup, and the affected-keys walk.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: the interviewer says 'We have 20 cache servers on hash % N and want to add 5 more for the holiday peak. What happens, and how would you do it instead?' Model answer (paraphrase freely): 'With hash % N, going from 20 to 21 servers moves about 20/21 of keys, so roughly 95% of the cache misses at once and the database takes the hit. I'd put servers and keys on a hash ring and look keys up with a binary search over the sorted server positions, wrapping at the top. When a server joins, only the keys between it and the server anticlockwise of it move, and they come from its clockwise neighbour, so each new server takes roughly 1/(N+1) of keys. With virtual nodes that work is split into small arcs pulled from many servers. I'd add the five servers one at a time and watch the miss rate.' Self-check boxes: 'I put a number on the % N damage (about N/(N+1))', 'I described lookup as clockwise / first position >= hash, with wrap', 'I said exactly which keys move on a join and where they come from'.

caveats: The N/(N+1) and 1/(N+1) figures assume hashes are uniformly random and, for the ring, that load is even (which needs virtual nodes, see Quest 5.2). On a basic ring with one random position per server, the amount that moves on a join can be far above or below 1/(N+1).

The book uses SHA-1 as its example hash. SHA-1 is broken for security uses (collisions have been found on purpose), but placement on a ring isn't a security feature, so that doesn't matter here. Real systems prefer fast non-cryptographic hashes such as Murmur3 (Cassandra) or used MD5 (Dynamo).

For a cache, 'moving' a key just means a miss and a refill from the database. For a database, the keys in the affected arc must actually be copied to the new owner before it starts serving them; the book's chapter stops at deciding which keys move.
The toy rings use 0..255 or 0..99 so every key is visible. Real rings have 2^64 to 2^160 positions and millions of keys.

quests.d: The two problems with the basic ring in numbers, why virtual nodes fix one of them, and who runs consistent hashing in production (Dynamo, Cassandra, Discord, Akamai, Maglev)
quests.goal: Your win today: you can name the two problems of the basic ring (uneven partitions and uneven keys) and put numbers on them, explain why virtual nodes help and what they cost (spread ~ 1/sqrt(V), more metadata), say honestly what consistent hashing does not fix (one hot key), and name five real systems that use it and what each one hashes.
quests.bookSections: Ch. 5: Two issues in the basic approach; Virtual nodes (spread and metadata trade-off); Wrap up (benefits: minimal redistribution, horizontal scaling, hotspot mitigation; real-world systems: Dynamo partitioning, Cassandra, Discord, Akamai CDN, Maglev load balancer).

stages.title: Crack #1: the lopsided ring
stages.teaches: Book's first issue: the partition (the arc between two adjacent servers) can't be kept the same size for every server once servers come and go, because positions are set by the hash, not by you. Even a perfect start breaks: 4 servers evenly spaced each own 25%; remove one and its clockwise neighbour now owns 50%, twice everyone else. Beyond the book, the math of random placement: with N servers at random positions, the expected largest arc is H_N / N of the ring, where H_N = 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/N. For N = 4 that's about 52% (fair share 25%); N = 10, about 29% (fair 10%); N = 100, about 5.2% (fair 1%). So the biggest server is overloaded by a factor of roughly ln N, and it gets worse, not better, as the cluster grows.
stages.interaction: A ring with share bars underneath (one bar per server, black line at fair share). Step 1: 4 servers evenly placed; the learner taps one to remove it and watches its neighbour's bar jump to 50%. Step 2 'You place it': a draggable new server; the learner drags it to rebalance (a 'Balance score' shows max share / fair share; reaching 1.0 is possible, placing at the middle of the big arc). Step 3 'The hash places it': a toggle switches to real mode, where the new server's position is hash(name); pressing 'Name a new server' (random names) drops it at a random spot, usually not where it's needed. Step 4 predict-then-watch: 'With 4 servers at random positions, how big is the largest arc on average?' options 'About 25%' / 'About 35%' / 'About 50%' (correct about 50%). Then a 'Roll 1,000 rings' button runs a quick Monte Carlo and shows the average largest arc (about 52%) next to the H_N/N formula; a small N selector (4, 10, 100) updates both.
stages.check: Prediction made and the Monte Carlo run; Q.quiz: 'In the book's example, one server is removed from an evenly spaced ring. What happens to its clockwise neighbour?' options 'Its partition doubles' / 'Its partition stays the same; keys spread evenly' / 'It loses its keys to the removed server' -> 'Its partition doubles'.

stages.title: Crack #2: unlucky keys
stages.sub: Uneven key distribution, and the hot key the ring can't fix
stages.teaches: Book's second issue: even with equal arcs, keys can bunch up, so one server holds most keys and another holds none. With few keys this is pure luck: with 4 equal arcs and 8 random keys, a given server is empty about 10% of the time ((3/4)^8), and at least one of the 4 is empty about 38% of the time; with 20 keys that drops to about 1.3%. Key-count noise shrinks as keys grow (relative spread about 1/sqrt(keys per server)), so with millions of keys, arc SIZE (crack #1) is what dominates. Separate problem: access skew. The book's wrap-up says consistent hashing helps with hotspot keys (e.g. a few celebrity accounts landing on one shard) by spreading data more evenly. Honest caveat (also in Quest 6.2): it helps when the hot data is many keys that happen to cluster; a single very hot key always hashes to exactly one spot, so one server serves it. That needs caching, read replicas or splitting the key, not more ring tricks.
stages.interaction: 'Throw the keys' sim: 4 servers with exactly equal arcs on a ring. A key-count selector (8 / 40 / 400 / 4,000) and a 'Throw' button scatter that many random keys onto the ring with a quick animation (for 4,000 just show dots fading in) and update per-server count bars plus 'max / average' readout. Predict-then-watch first: 'Throw 8 keys onto 4 equal arcs. How often does at least one server get zero keys?' options 'Almost never (under 5%)' / 'About 1 time in 3' / 'Almost always' -> about 1 in 3; then a 'Throw 1,000 times' button tallies how often a server came up empty (about 38%). Learner then throws 4,000 keys and sees max/average near 1.0. Final card 'The celebrity key': one key glows and receives 60% of all requests (a request-rate bar per server instead of a key-count bar); the learner tries pressing 'Add virtual nodes' and 'Add a server' and sees the hot server's request bar barely move; reveal the fix list (cache the hot key, replicate it, split it).
stages.check: Prediction made and simulation run at 4,000 keys; Q.quiz: 'One user's profile gets 50,000 reads per second and overloads one cache server. Does adding virtual nodes fix it?' options 'No: that one key still maps to one server; cache or replicate the key' / 'Yes: virtual nodes spread every key's traffic across all servers' / 'Yes, if you also switch to SHA-1' -> first.

stages.title: The patch, by the numbers
stages.sub: How many virtual nodes, and what they cost
stages.teaches: Book's fix: virtual nodes (also called replicas or tokens). Each real server is placed on the ring many times; a key goes to the first virtual node clockwise and therefore to its real server. More virtual nodes -> each server owns many small arcs whose sizes average out. The book reports a standard deviation of about 10% of the mean with 100 virtual nodes and about 5% with 200. Rule of thumb for random placement (beyond the book): a server's share is the sum of V random arcs, so its spread is about 1/sqrt(V): V = 25 -> 20%, V = 100 -> 10%, V = 400 -> 5%. Halving the spread costs 4x the virtual nodes. A quick simulation with 10 servers gives about 9% at 100 and about 6% at 200, so the book's 5% figure is on the optimistic side; the direction is the point. Cost: every virtual node is a ring entry that every router stores and that membership updates must ship around. Example: 1,000 servers x 256 virtual nodes = 256,000 entries; at about 24 bytes each (8-byte token + server ID) that's about 6 MB per copy, and lookups take about 18 comparisons. Heterogeneity: give a bigger server proportionally more virtual nodes. This quest does the math; the hands-on slider lab is Quest 6.2 stage 4 (link to lessons/0002-consistent-hashing.html#s4).
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check ladder (three cards, number inputs, tolerance +/-15%): (1) 'Target spread 20%. How many virtual nodes per server?' -> 25. (2) 'Target 5%?' -> 400. (3) 'Your cluster has 500 servers with 400 virtual nodes each. How many ring entries does every router hold?' -> 200,000; follow-up tap: 'about how many comparisons per lookup?' options 18 / 200 / 200,000 -> 18. Then a two-dial 'Trade-off meter': a V slider (1..1,000, log scale) drives two gauges side by side, 'Balance' (1/sqrt(V) spread) and 'Metadata' (entries x 24 bytes for a 1,000-server cluster). The learner must park the slider in a green zone where spread < 10% and metadata < 10 MB (V roughly 100 to 400). A small 'Want to drag real virtual nodes around? Quest 6.2, stage 4' link card.
stages.check: All three cards correct and the slider parked in the green zone; Q.quiz: 'You double the virtual nodes per server from 100 to 200. Roughly what happens to the load spread?' options 'It drops by about 30% (from ~10% to ~7%)' / 'It halves exactly' / 'It doesn't change' -> first.

stages.title: Who rides the ring
stages.sub: Five real systems, and one that isn't a ring at all
stages.teaches: Book's list of real users, with what each hashes: Amazon Dynamo: the partitioning component; the key's MD5 hash picks a coordinator node and the next distinct nodes clockwise hold replicas (the preference list; replication is Quest 6.3). Apache Cassandra: the partition key's Murmur3 token picks the nodes that own it; virtual nodes per node set by num_tokens (default 16 since 4.0, was 256). Discord: its Elixir backend uses a hash ring to decide which machine runs the process for a given server (guild) or user session, and it open-sourced its ring library (ex_hash_ring). Akamai CDN: the 1997 Karger et al. paper came from the MIT group that founded Akamai; the ring maps web objects (URLs) to cache servers so adding a cache doesn't flush everything. Google Maglev: a software network load balancer that hashes a connection's 5-tuple to pick a backend, so all packets of one connection reach the same backend. Twist: Maglev does not use a ring. It builds a fixed-size lookup table (size M, a prime; 65,537 in the paper): each backend has its own pseudo-random preference order of table slots (from an offset and a skip derived from its name), and backends take turns claiming their next free preferred slot. Every backend ends up with M/N slots give or take one (near-perfect balance), at the price of a little more disruption: when a backend leaves, a few slots can change hands between survivors too. Other non-ring alternatives worth naming: rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing and Google's jump consistent hash.
stages.interaction: Part A, matching: five system cards (Dynamo, Cassandra, Discord, Akamai, Maglev) to five 'what gets hashed -> what it picks' cards (key -> coordinator + replica nodes; partition key token -> owning nodes; guild/session ID -> which machine runs the process; URL/object -> which cache server; connection 5-tuple -> which backend server). Drag or tap-pair; wrong pair costs a heart with a one-line explanation. Part B, 'Build a Maglev table' mini-sim (toy example, not the paper's numbers): table size M = 7, three backends with preference lists B0 = [5, 0, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3] (offset 5, skip 2), B1 = [2, 1, 0, 6, 5, 4, 3] (offset 2, skip 6), B2 = [0, 3, 6, 2, 5, 1, 4] (offset 0, skip 3). The learner presses 'Next turn'; backends take turns B0, B1, B2, ... each claiming its next preferred slot that is still free. Before the fill, predict how many slots each gets (options '2/2/3 in some order' / '1/1/5' / '0/3/4' -> 2/2/3). Final table: slots 0..6 = B2, B1, B1, B2, B0, B0, B0. Then 'B1 dies' rebuilds with B0 and B2 only: B2, B0, B0, B2, B0, B0, B2. The learner taps slots that changed owner although their backend didn't die -> slot 6 (B0 -> B2). Caption: Maglev buys even balance (4/3 split) with a little extra disruption; a ring buys minimal disruption with less even balance.
stages.check: All five matches correct; Maglev prediction and the changed-slot tap done; Q.quiz: 'What does Maglev trade compared with a hash ring?' options 'More even load in exchange for a few extra slots moving when backends change' / 'Fewer keys moved in exchange for worse balance' / 'Nothing; it is a hash ring with a different name' -> first.

stages.title: Boss: The Ring Doctor
stages.sub: Diagnose the symptom, prescribe the fix
stages.teaches: Telling apart the problems this world covers: the rehashing problem (% N), crack #1 uneven arcs (virtual nodes or smarter token placement), crack #2 / hot key (not the ring's job), and balanced-but-correct situations where the right call is to leave it alone.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with 4 choices: { k: 'ring', label: 'Move to a ring', sub: 'stop using hash % N' }, { k: 'vn', label: 'More virtual nodes', sub: 'even out the arcs' }, { k: 'hot', label: 'Fix the hot key', sub: 'cache, replicate or split it' }, { k: 'ok', label: 'Working as designed', sub: 'leave it' }. Seven scenarios (none repeat Quest 6.2's): (1) A 10-node ring with one token each; after a node was decommissioned, one node stores 31% of the data -> vn. (2) A game leaderboard key 'global-top-100' gets 40% of all reads and its cache node runs at 100% CPU, the other nodes at 20% -> hot. (3) A 6-node cluster with 256 virtual nodes each: shares are 16.2%, 16.9%, 17.1%, 16.5%, 16.8%, 16.5% -> ok (fair is 16.7%, all within a few %). (4) A sharded session store uses user_id % 8; adding shard 9 logs every user out -> ring. (5) Brand-new tiny test cluster: 3 nodes, 9 keys, one node holds 6 of them -> ok (only 9 keys: that's luck, it evens out at scale). (6) A node with 2x the disk sits at 30% disk while the others are at 60% -> vn (give it twice the virtual nodes, heterogeneity). (7) When a basic-ring node crashes its neighbour's latency spikes, then the neighbour crashes too -> vn (spread the dead node's arcs across many servers). Outro: 'N changes -> ring. Arcs uneven or servers differ -> virtual nodes. One key on fire -> fix the key. A few percent of noise -> leave it.'
stages.check: Q.boss round completed under the engine's hearts rules.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.sub: The honest pitch for consistent hashing
stages.teaches: Model answer covering both cracks, the patch with its cost, the hot-key limit and real-world users.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: the interviewer asks 'Is consistent hashing enough to balance load in our cluster? What can still go wrong?' Model answer (paraphrase freely): 'The basic ring has two problems. Positions come from the hash, so arcs are uneven, and with N random servers the biggest can be ln N times the fair share; removing a server also dumps its arc on one neighbour. And keys can bunch up, though that evens out once there are lots of keys. Virtual nodes fix the arc problem: the spread is about 1 over the square root of the count, so a few hundred per server gets you to around 5 to 10%, at the cost of more ring metadata. Bigger servers get more virtual nodes. What it doesn't fix is a single hot key, which still lives on one server, so I'd cache or replicate that key. Dynamo, Cassandra, Discord and Akamai all use rings; Google's Maglev uses a lookup table instead to get even balance.' Self-check boxes: 'I named both problems of the basic ring', 'I gave virtual nodes with their cost (metadata)', 'I said hot keys still need another fix', 'I named at least two real systems'.

caveats: The H_N / N largest-arc figure and the 1/sqrt(V) spread are idealised maths for random placement. Real systems often place tokens deliberately: Dynamo moved to equal-sized fixed partitions (its 'Strategy 3'), and Cassandra 4.0's token allocation algorithm picks tokens to balance load, which is why 16 tokens per node is enough there.
The book's '5% at 200 virtual nodes' is on the optimistic side of a simple simulation (about 6 to 7%). Teach the trend (4x virtual nodes to halve the spread), not the exact number.
The book's wrap-up says consistent hashing mitigates the hotspot-key problem. That is true for many keys that cluster, not for one extremely hot key.

Discord and Akamai details are kept at the level their public write-ups support: Discord's hash ring routes processes across Elixir nodes; Akamai's roots are the Karger et al. caching work. Their current internals may differ.

Maglev in the stage is a toy (M = 7). The real table size is a large prime (65,537 in the paper), and Maglev also keeps a connection-tracking table so existing connections usually stick to their backend even when the lookup table changes.

quests.d: Full mock interview: design how a growing cache fleet decides which server holds each key
quests.goal: Your win today: given 'design consistent hashing' (framed as a cache fleet that grows and shrinks), you can run the 4-step interview: scope with the right questions, sketch the ring with clients, servers and a membership source, deep-dive virtual nodes, lookups and affected keys, survive the 'what if' curveballs, and close with the benefits, real-world users and honest limits.
quests.bookSections: Whole Ch. 5 through the book's 4-step framework (from Ch. 3): rehashing problem, ring, lookup, add/remove, two issues, virtual nodes, affected keys, wrap-up benefits and real-world users. Membership, replication and data-copy details are flagged as beyond-the-chapter extensions (replication links to Quest 6.3).

stages.title: Scope it
stages.teaches: The book's chapter has no scoping dialogue, so this quest frames it as an interviewer would: 'We run 20 cache servers in front of our database. Traffic doubles at peak, and we add and remove servers every day. Design how clients decide which server holds each key.' Good questions and the answers that become requirements: Is it a cache (a lost key is just a miss) or the system of record (data must be copied before cutover)? -> cache for now, store later. How often does membership change? -> daily, plus random failures. Are servers the same size? -> new ones are 2x bigger. How many keys and servers? -> ~500M keys, 20-60 servers. Are some keys much hotter than others? -> yes, a few celebrity profiles. Who does the routing, a client library or a proxy? -> your call. Requirements board (6): few keys move when servers change; even load; bigger servers carry more; a failed server's load spreads out; lookup is fast and local; hot keys don't melt one server.
stages.interaction: Same mechanic as 0008 stage 1: a 45-minute game clock bar, the 4-step framework strip, an interviewer chat, a requirements board with 6 slots and a deck of 10 question cards: 6 good (above) and 4 time-wasters ('Redis or Memcached?', 'Which programming language are the clients in?', 'Should we encrypt the keys?', 'What colour is the dashboard?'). Good questions cost 1 game-minute, pin a requirement and earn signal; time-wasters cost 3 minutes and signal with an interviewer reply like 'Let's park that.' Then a 30-second napkin check card: '500M keys over 20 servers, how many keys each?' -> 25M; 'adding the 21st server with a ring moves about how many keys in total?' -> about 24M (500M / 21); with % N about 476M (20/21). Number inputs, +/-15% tolerance.
stages.check: All 6 requirements pinned; napkin card answered; signal score shown.

stages.title: Sketch it
stages.sub: Step 2 · high-level design and buy-in (10-15 min)
stages.teaches: High-level design: clients carry a ring-aware library (or call a thin routing proxy); the ring is a sorted list of server positions; servers and keys are hashed with the same function; a key goes to the first server clockwise. Where does the ring come from? A small membership/config service (e.g. ZooKeeper or etcd) or gossip between nodes publishes the server list; clients rebuild their ring when it changes. Misses go to the database. Why not a central table of key -> server? 500M entries to store, update and query on every request; the ring needs only the server list.
stages.interaction: Whiteboard builder like 0008 stage 2: SVG canvas, tiles Clients, Ring library (or Router), Cache servers, Membership service, Database, plus 3 distractors ('hash(key) % N router', 'Central table of every key -> server', 'One giant cache server'). Tapping tiles in dependency order draws boxes and arrows; out-of-order costs a minute; a distractor costs a heart with a one-line reason. Then interviewer prompt 'Walk me through a lookup for key user:42': the learner orders 4 step cards (hash the key -> binary-search the sorted positions for the first >= hash -> wrap to the first position if none -> send the request to that server). Predict quiz: 'Two clients have different server lists for 2 seconds during a membership change. What happens?' options 'Some keys are briefly read from different servers, so a few extra misses' / 'All keys are lost' / 'Nothing; rings can't disagree' -> first.
stages.check: Diagram complete; lookup steps ordered; quiz answered.

stages.title: Deep dive: the ring, properly
stages.sub: Step 3 · virtual nodes, affected keys, heterogeneity
stages.teaches: Deep-dive points from the whole world: the two problems of the basic ring and virtual nodes as the fix (spread ~1/sqrt(V), 100-200 per server gives about 10%-5% in the book's numbers, more metadata); capacity-weighted virtual nodes for the 2x servers; finding affected keys on add/remove (anticlockwise to the previous server; with virtual nodes many small arcs from many servers); lookup as a binary search; replicas by continuing clockwise to the next distinct servers (Quest 6.3) if the cache later becomes a store; hot keys need replication or a local cache.
stages.interaction: Technique map like 0008 stage 3: 8 goal chips on the left, the learner taps the matching technique on the right. Pairs: 'Few keys move when a server joins' -> hash ring; 'Even share per server' -> many virtual nodes; '2x server carries 2x load' -> virtual nodes in proportion to capacity; 'Dead server's load spreads out' -> virtual nodes scattered around the ring; 'Know what to copy to a new node' -> walk anticlockwise from it to the previous position; 'Find the server fast' -> sorted positions + binary search; 'Keep copies on other servers' -> keep walking clockwise to the next distinct servers; 'One key gets 40% of reads' -> replicate/cache that key. Then the interviewer asks one twist: 'A new 2x server joins with 256 virtual nodes while others have 128. Roughly what share does it get in a 21-server cluster?' options about 2/22 (~9%) / about 1/21 (~5%) / about 50% -> ~9% (2 shares out of 20 + 2 = 22).

stages.title: Boss: the curveball barrage
stages.teaches: Mixed follow-ups from both quests of this world plus the key-value world.
stages.interaction: Curveball barrage like 0008 stage 4: 9 rapid scenario cards, 3 choices each; right = 1.5 game-minutes, wrong = heart + extra minute. Cards: (1) Ops wants to swap SHA-1 for Murmur3 -> nearly every key remaps; plan it as a full migration / dual-read warm-up. (2) A server reboots with a new IP and the ring hashes IPs -> it lands elsewhere; hash a stable server ID instead. (3) Two clients disagree on membership for a few seconds -> a few extra misses; converge via the membership service. (4) One server holds 30% with one token each -> add virtual nodes. (5) Leaderboard key gets 40% of reads -> cache/replicate the key; virtual nodes won't help. (6) 'Why not a lookup table of every key?' -> 500M entries to keep in sync; the ring stores only servers. (7) 'Why not just hash % N, we rarely resize?' -> fine only if N truly never changes; failures change N too. (8) A server dies under a basic ring and its neighbour then dies -> virtual nodes spread the load. (9) Now it's a database, not a cache: a node joins -> stream the affected arcs from their current owners before the new node serves them.
stages.check: Barrage completed with at least one heart left (engine rules).

stages.title: Wrap it up
stages.teaches: The book's wrap-up talking points, paraphrased: consistent hashing keeps redistribution minimal when servers join or leave; it makes horizontal scaling easy because data spreads more evenly; it helps with hotspot shards. Real-world users: Dynamo's partitioning, Cassandra's data partitioning, Discord, the Akamai CDN, Google's Maglev load balancer. Strong closers add the honest limits (one hot key, metadata cost of virtual nodes) and alternatives (rendezvous hashing, jump hash, Maglev's table).
stages.interaction: Like 0008 stage 5: 7 closing-move cards; the learner picks exactly 3 and presses 'Deliver my close'. Strong: 'Recap: minimal key movement, even load, easy horizontal scaling', 'Name real users: Dynamo, Cassandra, Discord, Akamai, Maglev', 'Honest limits: a single hot key and virtual-node metadata; mention rendezvous/jump/Maglev as alternatives'. Weak: 'Re-derive SHA-1 from scratch', 'Say: and that's consistent hashing, done', 'Propose moving everything to one big server', 'List every hash function you know'. Score by number of strong picks; the interviewer chat reacts to each.
stages.check: Close delivered with at least 2 strong moves.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: The whole chapter in one answer.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'Summarise your design for routing keys to cache servers in 60 seconds.' Model answer (paraphrase freely): 'hash % N remaps about N/(N+1) of keys whenever the fleet changes, so I'd use consistent hashing. Servers and keys are hashed into the same large space bent into a ring; a key belongs to the first server clockwise, found by binary search over the sorted positions. A join or leave only moves the keys in one arc, about k/n of them, and I can compute exactly which ones by walking anticlockwise to the previous position. The basic ring is uneven, so each server gets a few hundred virtual nodes, more for bigger machines, which also spreads a failed server's load. Clients get the server list from a membership service. A single hot key still needs caching or replication. This is what Dynamo and Cassandra do for partitioning.' Self-check boxes: 'I said why not % N, with a number', 'I described the ring + clockwise lookup', 'I covered virtual nodes and capacity weighting', 'I named a limit (hot key) and a real system'. Then the scorecard (signal, time used, hearts) is shown and stored under a separate key sdq:v1:0503-interview, like 0008.

caveats: Chapter 5 is a concept chapter, not a full 'design X' problem, so the cache-fleet framing, scoping dialogue and membership service are this quest's additions; say so in the intro.
Membership (how clients learn the server list) is outside the book's chapter. ZooKeeper/etcd or gossip are common choices; the key-value world (Quest 6.6) covers gossip.
For a database rather than a cache, a joining node must receive its arcs' data before it serves them; the book doesn't cover the copy protocol.
Hot-key caveat and the optimistic 5% virtual-node figure, as in Quest 5.2.

cheatsheetOutline: One page, 'World 5 - Consistent Hashing', with a banner linking to Quest 6.2 (lessons/0002-consistent-hashing.html) for the hands-on ring and virtual-node lab. Section 5.1 Ring Math: serverIndex = hash(key) % N and the rehashing problem (cache-miss storm); move fractions table: % N moves N/(N+1) on add, (N-1)/N on remove (4->5: 80%, 20->21: 95%, 99->100: 99%) vs ring ~1/(N+1) and 1/N, k/n rule; hash space 0..2^160-1 for SHA-1 (~1.46e48), MD5 128-bit in Dynamo, Murmur3 -2^63..2^63-1 in Cassandra; arc share = ((pos - prev) mod S) / S; lookup = sorted positions + binary search for first >= hash, wrap to first (18 comparisons for 256k positions); affected keys: add -> anticlockwise from new server to previous, taken from clockwise neighbour; remove -> anticlockwise from removed server to previous, given to clockwise neighbour; with virtual nodes many small arcs from many servers; traps: changing hash function or hashing unstable IPs. Section 5.2 Cracks in the Ring: crack 1 uneven partitions (remove one of 4 even servers -> neighbour 50%; random largest arc ~ H_N/N: 52% at N=4, 29% at N=10, 5.2% at N=100); crack 2 uneven keys (8 keys on 4 arcs: some server empty ~38%); hot single key is not fixed by the ring; virtual nodes: spread ~1/sqrt(V), book 10% at 100 and 5% at 200, metadata = servers x V entries, capacity-weighted V; real users table: Dynamo (key -> coordinator + preference list), Cassandra (Murmur3 token, num_tokens 16 since 4.0), Discord (guild/session -> Elixir node, ex_hash_ring), Akamai (URL -> cache server, Karger 1997), Maglev (5-tuple -> backend via prime-size lookup table; even balance, slight extra disruption); alternatives: rendezvous, jump hash. Boss: 4-step strip with minute ranges; 6 scoping questions -> 6 requirements; final diagram (clients + ring library -> cache servers, membership service, database on miss); 60-second answer; curveball one-liners.
